steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper studying gender bias in chemical named entity recognition models, using both synthetic template data and a new real-world dataset with self-identified gender. Motivate the problem, position it against prior bias work, and list the contributions.

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Chemical named entity recognition (NER) means extracting chemical mentions (e.g., drug names) from text. Chemical NER is needed for many downstream tasks, from pharmacovigilance to helping drug discovery by mining biomedical research articles. For example, Chemical NER systems are the first step in the pipelines that are developed to mine adverse drug reactions (ADRs). But we do not know if these systems perform the same for everyone. Who benefits from them, and who can be harmed? In this paper we present a comprehensive analysis of the gender-related performance disparities of Chemical NER systems.

Performance disparities have gotten a lot of attention recently in NLP. For example, text classification models differ across sub-populations such as gender, race and minority dialects. Performance disparities can show up in many parts of NLP systems, including the pre-trained models (e.g., word embeddings) and their downstream applications. Previous research has looked at these disparities for NER systems, but mostly on synthetic data and non-biomedical NER applications. Our study fills this gap with a comprehensive examination of gender-related performance disparities in Chemical NER, on both synthetic and real-world data.

This paper is most similar to earlier work on gender bias in NER, but there are two main differences. First, we focus on Chemical NER, which is a less studied area in Biomedical NLP even though it has major bias implications. Second, that work uses synthetic data and templates (e.g., NAME in LOCATION) for the bias analysis, while we go deeper and also analyze how morphology patterns interact with bias. For example, another study found a preference for linguistically feminine brand names in the market, and this led drug companies to adopt naming conventions like this. Patterns like these in the training data can cause models to misclassify female names as chemicals without anyone intending it.

- real-world data: performance on groups identifying as male/female; women prescribed antidepressants more often than men; gender differences in pain sensitivity and opioid prescriptions (women get opioids twice as often); if models miss often-mentioned drugs -> gender-specific bias
- dual approach: template data + novel annotated real-world dataset with self-identified gender; synthetic targets specific biases (morphology); self-identified data more realistic (how people write, what they write about)
- contributions:
  1. novel annotated Chemical NER dataset for social media with self-identified gender; first Reddit-based; first with self-identified gender
  2. testing framework for gender bias in Chemical NER on synthetic and real data; first bias analysis for chemical NER models

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Chemical named entity recognition (NER) means extracting chemical mentions (e.g., drug names) from text. Chemical NER is needed for many downstream tasks, from pharmacovigilance to helping drug discovery by mining biomedical research articles. For example, Chemical NER systems are the first step in the pipelines that are developed to mine adverse drug reactions (ADRs). But we do not know if these systems perform the same for everyone. Who benefits from them, and who can be harmed? In this paper we present a comprehensive analysis of the gender-related performance disparities of Chemical NER systems.

Performance disparities have gotten a lot of attention recently in NLP. For example, text classification models differ across sub-populations such as gender, race and minority dialects. Performance disparities can show up in many parts of NLP systems, including the pre-trained models (e.g., word embeddings) and their downstream applications. Previous research has looked at these disparities for NER systems, but mostly on synthetic data and non-biomedical NER applications. Our study fills this gap with a comprehensive examination of gender-related performance disparities in Chemical NER, on both synthetic and real-world data.

This paper is most similar to earlier work on gender bias in NER, but there are two main differences. First, we focus on Chemical NER, which is a less studied area in Biomedical NLP even though it has major bias implications. Second, that work uses synthetic data and templates (e.g., NAME in LOCATION) for the bias analysis, while we go deeper and also analyze how morphology patterns interact with bias. For example, another study found a preference for linguistically feminine brand names in the market, and this led drug companies to adopt naming conventions like this. Patterns like these in the training data can cause models to misclassify female names as chemicals without anyone intending it.

We also look at real-world data, checking how chemical NER systems perform on groups that identify as male or female. For example, one study shows that women are prescribed antidepressants more often than men. Other studies show gender differences in pain sensitivity and in opioid prescriptions, with women getting opioids twice as often. If chemical NER models have trouble detecting the drugs that are often mentioned, this may cause gender-specific biases in how they perform. Our analysis finds some of these patterns in real data.

Overall, this paper has a dual approach: we explore template data, but we also put together and annotate a novel real-world dataset with self-identified gender information. With synthetic data we can target specific biases in the models (e.g., morphological issues). And we think that exploring data from people who self-identified their demographic information gives a more realistic understanding of how these models will perform, based on how people write and what they write about.

Our main contributions are two:

- 1. We introduce a novel annotated Chemical NER dataset for social media data. The dataset also contains self-identified gender information that can be used to measure gender bias in Chemical NER models. As far as we know, this is the first Reddit-based Chemical NER dataset, and it is also the first Chemical NER dataset with self-identified gender information.

- 2. We provide a comprehensive testing framework for gender bias in Chemical NER, using both synthetic and real-world data. As far as we know, our results are the first bias analysis for chemical NER models. This allows a better understanding of modern chemical NER techniques.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Chemical named entity recognition (NER) is the extraction of chemical mentions (e.g., drug names) from text. Chemical NER is essential in many downstream tasks, from pharmacovigilance [1] to facilitating drug discovery by mining biomedical research articles [2]. For instance, Chemical NER systems are the first step in pipelines developed to mine adverse drug reactions (ADRs) [3,4]. However, it is unknown whether these systems perform the same for everyone. Who benefits from these systems, and who can be harmed? In this paper, we present a comprehensive analysis of gender-related performance disparities of Chemical NER systems.

Performance disparities have recently received substantial attention in NLP. For example, text classification models show differences across sub-populations such as gender, race, and minority dialects [5,6,7,8,9,10]. Performance disparities can manifest in multiple parts of NLP systems, including the pre-trained models (e.g., word embeddings) and their downstream applications [11,12,13]. While previous research has explored these disparities for NER systems, the focus has largely been on synthetic data and non-biomedical NER applications [14]. Our study addresses this gap with a comprehensive examination of gender-related performance disparities in Chemical NER, on both synthetic and real-world data.

This paper is most similar to [14], with two primary distinctions. First, we focus on Chemical NER, a less studied area in Biomedical NLP despite its major bias implications. Second, while [14] uses synthetic data and templates (e.g., NAME in LOCATION) for bias analysis, we go deeper, including an analysis of how morphology patterns interact with bias. For instance, [15] highlighted a preference for linguistically feminine brand names in the market, which led drug companies to adopt such naming conventions. Such patterns in training data can inadvertently cause models to misclassify female names as chemicals.

We also examine real-world data, looking at the performance of chemical NER systems on groups that identify as male or female. For instance, [16] shows that women are prescribed antidepressants more frequently than men. Other studies, like [17], reveal gender differences in pain sensitivity and opioid prescriptions, with women receiving opioids twice as often. If chemical NER models struggle to detect the drugs that are often mentioned, this may cause gender-specific biases in their performance. Our analysis identifies some of these patterns in real data.

Overall, this paper takes a dual approach: we explore template data, but we also assemble and annotate a novel real-world dataset with self-identified gender information. Synthetic data allows us to target specific biases in the models (e.g., morphological issues). Likewise, we believe that exploring data from people who have self-identified their demographic information provides a more realistic understanding of how these models will perform, based on how people write and what they write about.

Our main contributions are two-fold:

- 1. We introduce a novel annotated Chemical NER dataset for social media data. The dataset also contains self-identified gender information that can be used to measure gender bias in Chemical NER models. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first Reddit-based Chemical NER dataset, and the first Chemical NER dataset with self-identified gender information.

- 2. We provide a comprehensive testing framework for gender bias in Chemical NER using both synthetic and real-world data. To the best of our knowledge, our results are the first bias analysis of chemical NER models. This allows a better understanding of modern chemical NER techniques.
